Members of the transport group MANIBELA hold placards and chant slogans on the second day of a nationwide jeepney strike at their headquarters in Manila on Thursday, March 26.

The group called on the national government to prioritize the removal of excise tax and value-added tax (VAT) on fuel and to consider repealing the Oil Deregulation Law. It added that around 100,000 transport workers across the country have joined the ongoing protest. 

📸: Mark Balmores/MB

Delivery riders and drivers line up to claim financial assistance at the Kartilya ng Katipunan in Manila on Thursday, March 26.

A total of 21,127 beneficiaries are set to receive ₱5,000 each under the Department of Social Welfare and Development’s Assistance to Individuals in Crisis Situations (AICS) program, with support from the Manila Department of Social Welfare and Development, the Manila Traffic and Parking Bureau, and the Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board (LTFRB).

📸: Mark Balmores/MB

data.raw_text:
PGMN Anchor @TransportGuy reflects on how the recent fuel price surge coincided with a noticeable easing of traffic on major roads, highlighting a shift in travel behavior during the crisis . The observation adds to ongoing discussions on congestion in Metro Manila, as rising costs appear to be influencing how often and why people choose to be on the road, even as transport-dependent sectors continue to face pressure.

He situates this within broader policy considerations, pointing to measures such as temporary fuel tax relief and stricter implementation of telecommuting policies. The situation underscores how both economic conditions and regulatory choices can shape mobility patterns, raising questions on how similar improvements in traffic flow can be sustained without relying on external shocks.
